cards.text: This one's a psalm of the sons of Korah, written for the choirmaster. And it opens LOUD, telling people to hear this and listen. Friend, that's somebody tapping a glass before a toast, and the WHOLE room goes quiet.

cards.question: The writer wants people to hear this. How far does his call to listen reach?

answers.text: Everyone in the world rich and poor alike
Everyone in Israel from the least to greatest
The rich and the powerful in every land

cards.text: Then the writer says his mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of his heart will bring understanding. He'll incline his ear to a proverb.

cards.question: Wisdom and understanding are on the way. How does the writer say he'll express his riddle?

cards.text: So here's the riddle. In times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround him, why should he be afraid?

cards.question: The wicked usurpers surrounding the writer are leaning hard on something. What do they trust in?

cards.text: Yep, they trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches. Never had that problem myself, friend, because my WHOLE price tag was 25 cents.

cards.question: True or false: with enough money, a man can redeem his brother by paying his ransom to God.

cards.text: The redemption of a soul is costly, and no payment would ever be enough. That's a price tag even the guy who mentions his boat in EVERY conversation can't cover.

cards.question: No payment could ever be enough to redeem a soul. What would that payment be trying to buy?

answers.text: A seat in the king's own court

cards.text: Now look around, friend. The writer says it's clear that the wise man and the fool end up the same way.

cards.question: The writer says it's clear that wise men ___ just like the foolish and the senseless.
When the foolish and the senseless perish, what happens to all their wealth?

cards.text: Some of these folks even had their lands named after them. The Millers carved my name on a handle, and I STILL ended up in a junk drawer.

cards.question: Their lands carried their names, but the writer says their ___ are their eternal homes.
True or false: the writer says that despite his wealth, a man cannot endure.

cards.text: All that wealth, and he still can't endure. The writer says he's like the beasts that perish.
The writer looks back at everything he just said and calls it the fate of the foolish. Then, Selah.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says this fate is for the foolish only, and not for the followers who endorse their sayings.

cards.text: Then he paints a picture, and it gets DARK. The foolish are like sheep, destined for Sheol.

cards.question: The foolish are like sheep destined for Sheol. Who does the writer say will be their shepherd?
The writer says that in the morning, the ___ will rule over the foolish.

cards.text: Their form decays in Sheol, far from their lofty abode. Then the writer drops one little word that flips the whole psalm: But.

cards.question: The foolish are headed for Sheol. So who does the writer say will redeem HIS life from Sheol?
True or false: the writer says God will surely take him to Himself.

cards.text: Selah. Somebody reached into a dark junk drawer for me once, friend, so that line gets me EVERY time. Then the writer turns to the listener with some advice about a man whose house keeps getting fancier.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says to be afraid when a man grows rich and the splendor of his house increases.
So why shouldn't you be afraid when a man grows rich?

answers.text: When he dies he carries nothing away
His riches will soon be stolen from him
He will lose it all before he grows old

cards.text: His abundance will not follow him down. Friend, I have NEVER seen a moving truck following a hearse.
In his lifetime he blesses his own soul. And the writer adds that men praise you when you prosper.

cards.question: The rich man blessed his own soul in his lifetime. But when he dies, who does he join?

cards.text: And that generation of his fathers will never see the light of day.

cards.question: In the last line, the man who is like the beasts that perish is the one with riches but without ___.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 1 mentions toast, a food that isn't a cookie and isn't in the passage.

rule.text: In jokes and comparisons, cookies are the only food he mentions.

findings.problem: The setup gives the baker no basis for choosing a harp over a trumpet or a scroll. This is an arbitrary detail of the line, not something a thoughtful baker can reason out from the earlier cards.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The question begins with 'Their' without saying whose lands and homes these are. The antecedent depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The phrase 'this fate' does not explain what fate is being discussed. Without the preceding story card, the question lacks the context needed to stand on its own.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Nothing in the sheep and Sheol setup establishes who will rule in the morning, and 'upright' has not appeared in the earlier cards. The blank therefore asks for unseen wording rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: This is a 'who' question, but 'His own wisdom' is not the same kind of answer as God Himself and the king of Israel. The three options do not form a consistent set of possible persons.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This non-opening story card has three sentences: 'Selah.', Papa Dorin's personal response, and the transition to the advice in verse 16. It needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.
